newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ivory Coast hints at Boutros-Ghali succession bid.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast hints at Boutros-Ghali succession bid.

text.p: President Henri Konan Bedie hinted on Tuesday that Ivory Coast stood ready to offer its foreign minister, Amara Essy, as a candidate for secretary-general of the United Nations if Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali stands down.

The United States last week vetoed a second five-year term for Boutros-Ghali, 74, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister, but he refused to withdraw and no African nation has yet put forward an alternative.
Konan Bedie said after talks with French President Jacques Chirac during a private visit to Paris that it was too early to present another candidate.

"For the moment, Ivory Coast has not registered its candidacy," the president said. But he added that Essy would be "entirely up to the task", noting that he had been president of the U.N. General Assembly.
"There has been no Ivorian declaration of intention so far. I believe it is appropriate to wait for African heads of state in the Organisaiton of African Unity to do their work," Konan Bedie said.
Chirac pressed for Boutros-Ghali to be reappointed and warned that France would veto any candidate who was not a fluent French-speaker.
African states, encouraged by France, have so far remained firm in supporting Boutros-Ghali, despite impatience by the United States and some other Security Council members.
But in a letter revealed on Tuesday, Ethiopia broke ranks and urged Africa to abandon the embattled secretary-general and present alternative candidates for his job.
Under the U.N. system of rotation among the continents, the world's poorest continent would normally be entitled to a second term at the helm.

Other African candidates who have been canvassed include Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; Salim A. Salim of Tanzania, secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity; and Olara Otunnu, a former Ugandan U.N. envoy who heads the New York-based International Peace Academy.
